_about: Annotated-reading segments appended to each lecture clip. Each beat is narrated (narration key r<N>_b<i>, made by ../make_narration.py) while a pen marks phrases of the passage with Rough Notation and writes margin notes in Hershey script. Colours follow PenMentor's teacher pens: green = key idea, red = watch out / common mistake, blue = definition or term, yellow = highlight. Every phrase must appear verbatim in the passage.

NextWordVideo.title: How Language Models Write
passage: When you ask a chatbot a question, it does not look the answer up in a list of facts. A large language model writes its reply one small piece at a time.
For each next token, the model gives every token it knows a probability. Then it samples: it picks one, with likely tokens picked more often.
But "likely to come next" is not the same as "true".

beats.say: Now let's read the key passage with a pen. First: the model does not look the answer up.

marks.phrase: does not look the answer up in a list of facts

note.near: does not look the answer up in a list of facts

beats.say: The key idea: every token gets a probability.
Then it samples. Likely tokens are picked more often, but not every time.

marks.phrase: with likely tokens picked more often

note.near: with likely tokens picked more often

beats.say: And the sentence to remember: likely is not the same as true.

BiasVideo.title: Bias In, Bias Out
passage: If some kinds of examples are rare in the training data, the model often learns them poorly.
An overall accuracy is an average across everyone tested. If one group is small, its failures barely move the average.
More data helps only if it covers the missing group.

beats.say: Let's read this with a pen. Examples that are rare in the training data are learned poorly.
An overall accuracy is an average, and a small group's failures barely move it.

marks.phrase: its failures barely move the average

note.near: its failures barely move the average

beats.say: And the fix: more data helps only if it covers the missing group.

ClaimsVideo.title: Checking Claims and Sources
passage: A citation is itself a claim: it can be wrong, or point to something that does not exist.
Supported: the source says the same thing. Contradicted: the source says something different. No real source: the cited source, page or section cannot be found.
Professional fact-checkers do not just read a page closely; they leave it to see what other sources say about the claim and about the source.

beats.say: Pen out. First line: a citation is itself a claim.

marks.phrase: A citation is itself a claim

note.near: A citation is itself a claim

beats.say: Three stamps for each claim: supported, contradicted, and no real source.
And the fact-checkers' habit: they leave the page to see what other sources say.

DataTrailVideo.title: Your Data Trail
passage: Everything you type into a chatbot leaves your device.
You cannot always control the second part, but you always control the first: what you put in.
Deleting a chat from your list may not remove every copy.
Data minimization means sharing only what the task needs.

beats.say: Mark this first. Everything you type leaves your device.
But one thing is always yours to control: what you put in.
Deleting a chat may not remove every copy.
So practise data minimization: share only what the task needs.

marks.phrase: sharing only what the task needs

WhatIsAIVideo.title: What Counts as AI?
passage: A calculator follows fixed rules. A spam filter learns from millions of emails that people marked as spam, and it keeps adjusting.
When you ask "is this AI?", a useful test is: did the system learn its behavior from examples?
Every system above is narrow AI: it is built for one kind of task.

beats.say: Let's mark up the definition. Fixed rules on one side, learning from examples on the other.
Here is the test to remember.

marks.phrase: did the system learn its behavior from examples?

note.near: did the system learn its behavior from examples?

beats.say: And the name for the tools you use today: narrow A I, built for one kind of task.

marks.phrase: built for one kind of task

StrengthsVideo.title: Strengths and Limits
passage: It is very good at producing plausible language. It is not built to guarantee that what it writes is accurate.
Notice the pattern: these are tasks where you can judge the result.
Before using an AI output, ask: how would I know if this were wrong?

beats.say: Pen out. Plausible language, yes. Guaranteed accuracy, no.
The pattern behind the good uses: tasks where you can judge the result.

marks.phrase: tasks where you can judge the result

note.near: tasks where you can judge the result

beats.say: And the question to ask every time.

marks.phrase: how would I know if this were wrong?

note.near: how would I know if this were wrong?

TrainingDataVideo.title: Learning from Data
passage: During training, the model adjusts millions of internal numbers until its guesses match the labels as often as possible. It is not memorizing each photo; it is finding patterns that separate cats from dogs.
A model generalizes well to new examples that resemble its training data.
Each choice affects who the system works well for.

beats.say: Let's annotate. Training means adjusting numbers until the guesses match the labels.
Not memorizing photos, but finding patterns.
It generalizes to new examples that resemble its training data.
And every data choice affects who the system works well for.

marks.phrase: Each choice affects who the system works well for

FiveQuestionsVideo.title: Accurate for Whom?
passage: Who was it tested on? Do the test groups resemble the people it will be used on?
A false positive says a student's own writing was AI-generated. A false negative misses AI-written text.
Human oversight means a person with authority reviews AI outputs that affect people, can override them, and is accountable for the final decision.

beats.say: With the pen: question one comes first.
Two kinds of error, with different costs.
And real oversight has three parts: authority, the power to override, and accountability.

DelegateVideo.title: What to Hand to AI
passage: Delegating support work can save time. Delegating core work can mean you skip the learning the course is for, even when the result looks good.
Is this the skill the assignment is meant to build? If yes, keep it, and use AI for feedback or practice instead.
Whatever you delegate, you decide what to keep, change or throw away, and you are responsible for what you submit.

If it is the skill being built, keep it, and use A I for feedback instead.

beats.say: And you are responsible for what you submit.

ClearRequestVideo.title: Writing a Clear Request
passage: A model can only work with what you give it. Vague requests get generic answers.

I'm a first-year biology student preparing for a quiz. I understand the light reactions but not the Calvin cycle. Explain it in plain language in under 150 words, step by step. Then give me three practice questions with the answers at the end.
Treat the first reply as a draft.

beats.say: Let's mark the clear request, part by part. The goal.
The context.

marks.phrase: I understand the light reactions but not the Calvin cycle

beats.say: The constraints, and the format.

marks.phrase: in plain language in under 150 words, step by step
three practice questions with the answers at the end

beats.say: And remember: the first reply is a draft.

DisclosureVideo.title: Integrity and Disclosure
passage: Integrity means following the rules of the course you are in and being honest about what you did.
A good disclosure says what tool, for what, and what you did with the output.
If your work is questioned, your drafts, notes and AI-use record are the best evidence of your process.

PlanVideo.title: Your AI Use Plan
passage: Tasks I will use AI for: two or three support tasks where AI helps you and you can check the result.
Tasks I will keep: the skills your program is meant to build, which you will do yourself.
Your plan should change as tools, courses and policies change.
